item.title: When Trusting People Is a Struggle
item.description:
Perfectionism

When Trusting People Is a Struggle

Perfectionists' extreme standards for others can make it difficult to trust.

Posted July 30, 2026

Key points
  • Perfectionists tend to try to discover another's essential nature to know for sure if they can trust them.
  • Forming a conclusion about another's essence tends to be distorted by biased thinking.
  • We can learn to tolerate ambiguity, reframing it as a fact of life, rather than a mental nuisance.

At its core, perfectionism is extremely personal, often aiming to touch one’s essence, whether one’s own or another’s. The perfectionist’s search may appear secular, but it could even be considered spiritual in nature, even if the individual defines themself as an atheist or agnostic; regardless, they often seek fundamental, personal truths. If the primary motive of their life is becoming perfect, this may stem from a desperate need to conclusively and directly answer the questions: “Who am I really?” “Who am I at my core?” “Am I really defective?” And one way to get closer to these truths, eliminating confusion, is by testing one’s abilities or traits. “If I’m brilliant, then I should always thrive academically.” “If I’m beautiful, then I should never be sexually or romantically rejected.”

Even grander, the assumptions may be, “If I’m lovable, then I should find true love,” or “If I’m brilliant, then my work should be universally applauded.” Since no achievement can ever really “prove” who you are, we keep upping the ante, hoping the next one will. The search is for certainty—which, to borrow from F. Scott Fitzgerald’s The Great Gatsby, seems to recede whenever we think we’re drawing near it—life presents all of us with few absolutes.

The fixation on a core self often plagues the perfectionist in several respects: the first is related to poor self-esteem, and the second is associated with one’s relationships. Self-oriented perfectionism implies holding oneself to an extremely high standard while other-oriented perfectionism implies holding others to it. Often, perfectionists are both self- and other-oriented. So, they create tests for themselves and others. And those tests are often brutal. In treatment, a perfectionist may note all of the reasons why they can’t trust others. Cynically, they may only recall instances of betrayal from them, highlighting the stark contrast between their expectations and reality. For example, a perfectionist, griping about the struggles in their burgeoning but already unsteady romantic relationship may remark, “I can’t believe this is who they really are.”

How the Search for Essence Leads to Cognitive Biases

However, the preoccupation with discovering another’s essence fails us in several ways. First, when assessing the source of a failure (regardless of its type), we tend to be biased. Cognitive psychology teaches us about ‘the fundamental attribution error.’ When another person fails an exam or to act morally, we tend to blame their essence. We’ll say something like, “You see, he’s just lazy.” We believe a test, whatever it may be, proves something about who they “really are.” Yet, we blame our own failures, paradoxically, solely on our circumstances. So, we may believe our true essence wasn’t allowed to shine because something impeded its revelation. They failed because they’re lazy, but we failed because the exam was unfair or we had too much to juggle, which is also unfair. In reality, the fundamental attribution error indicates how unfair our subjective tests or at least our evaluations of their results frequently are.

article continues after advertisement

Second, based on our insight of the mentioned mental error, we may also conclude that, on the whole, failings, whether moral or otherwise, are multi-determined, based on multiple causes, which include our tendencies. The judge, who’s unfortunately engaged in flawed thinking, isn’t necessarily wrong in their conclusions; it’s that each conclusion indicates only part of that causal system. This implies that the question of whether someone is or isn’t trustworthy (or good) is likely going to have a more complicated answer than the conclusions we tend to quickly form about who others are.

Third, social scientist Christian Miller, whose work illuminates the nature and frequency of integrity, concluded, “Our hearts are not morally pure, but they are not morally corrupt either. Rather, they are a messy blend of good and evil.” His research indicates that most of us are morally average. We tend to make better choices when we know someone else is watching or when reminded of some agreement we made. Otherwise, we can easily lie or cheat. Combine these insights with a need for clarity, general indecisiveness, a chronic state of confusion, and a penchant for black-and-white thinking, and it’s easy to see why an appeal to essences is preferable to a perfectionist, and why testing is the preferred method. Perfectionists use tests to form simple assumptions, thereby alleviating their anxiety and confusion. Yet, we’re all bound to fail these tests, especially the moral ones, according to Miller, occasionally. So, perfectionists often isolate themselves from most, if not all, others until they can somehow prove to them they’re good at heart.

Challenging Perfectionist Beliefs

Yet, it’s as much the perfectionist’s responsibility to grab a hold of their own beliefs. In treatment, a perfectionist may remark, “I was hoping you’d finally tell me something that would make me forgive and/or trust others.” Like the wizard in The Wizard of Oz, therapy isn’t capable of producing magic beyond the curtain; it merely challenges you to decide for yourself what “good enough” evidence is. Does another always need to fit your definition of loyalty? Are they never allowed to falter? And what if they can’t prove how much they care for and love you? Perhaps, them trying, in general, is good enough. Perhaps, you’ll never touch their essence, but you’ll allow yourself to experience their genuine attempts at consistency. Perhaps, you’ll temporarily halt your line of inquiry into their soul to feel what it’s like just being near them. As therapists, we can’t make anyone trust anyone else, but we can challenge the cognitive system used solely to justify and perpetuate self-isolation.

My last thought: Remember not only that you’re responsible for what you believe but also that you don’t have all of the time in the world to make up your mind. This means you can’t spend your entire life trying to concretely prove that someone is essentially good and trustworthy. We often have to take somewhat of a leap of faith and learn to tolerate ambiguity, our chronic state of confusion, by accepting it as an existential limitation (for any human), rather than a mental flaw needing a quick resolution.

item.title: Recalling Isaac Prilleltensky’s Psychopolitical Validity
item.description:
Career

Recalling Isaac Prilleltensky’s Psychopolitical Validity

Seeing work through the lenses of epistemic and transformative validity.

Posted July 30, 2026

Key points
  • Psychopolitical validity is a framework from the field of community psychology.
  • It explores the role of power and politics in psychological research and action.
  • Epistemic validity asks whether psychological research fully understands how power operates.

Authored by Miles Thompson and Ecesu Keskin

This post is about a framework within community psychology called "psychopolitical validity,” proposed by Isaac Prilleltensky. Below, there is a brief overview of the framework and its two main lenses: i. “Epistemic validity” and ii. “Transformative validity."

While the original idea is over 20 years old, this piece is being written now as both Isaac, and his wife Ora, died in May 2026. There is already a touching tribute to Isaac elsewhere on Psychology Today, as well as on the website of the University of Miami. More about him and his work can be found on his personal website. But this piece simply seeks to amplify his ideas around psychopolitical validity.

Why Psychopolitical Validity?

In his 2003 and 2008 articles, Prilleltensky introduces psychopolitical validity (PPV) as a framework. As the article titles note, there was an original focus on: understanding, challenging and overcoming oppression (2003), and later a focusing more broadly on the role of power in wellness, oppression and liberation (2008).

Fundamentally, PPV encourages community psychologists and psychologists more generally to place an understanding of power and politics at the center of their psychological research and action. The framework emphasizes the importance of integrating psychological and political dimensions, recognizing that psychological knowledge and practice itself is shaped by social, political and institutional forces.

Prilleltensky argues that psychological and political perspectives can often be looked at in isolation and can be incomplete on their own. Moreover, that psychology can tend to view suffering mainly through an individual lens, downplaying the role of social, economic and political arrangements. As such, more work is needed to explore how power and politics influence psychological well-being and suffering. PPV aims to bridge the gap between what community psychology as a field aspires to do and what it is able to achieve—by evaluating the work it produces using the lens of epistemic and transformative validity.

Epistemic validity refers to the depth and accuracy with which researchers understand how power and politics impacts the situations they are trying to influence. The term epistemic relates to ‘epistemology.’ Both come from the Greek, ‘episteme,’ meaning ‘knowledge.’ Epistemic validity therefore explores the level of understanding shown in terms of power and politics. Not just in abstract terms, but in terms of how it can operate—both negatively and positively—across personal, relational and collective domains. For example:

  • Personal: powerlessness or agency.
  • Relational: discrimination or mutual support.
  • Collective: exploitative institutions or fully democratic participation.

Examining how power operates at these personal, relational and collective levels is one of the core features of PPV.

In short, epistemic validity asks whether any research sufficiently accounts for how power and politics impacts the human experience and how it shapes wellness, oppression and liberation. In this way, it seeks to move research beyond simply describing distress to examining the wider contextual conditions that produce it.

Transformative validity shifts the focus from understanding power, to challenging it. It asks whether research is likely to produce meaningful change. Prilleltensky (2008) cautions that too often “community psychology interventions, however well intentioned, do not alter structures, but rather help their victims” (p.130). PPV challenges researchers and practitioners to go beyond understanding oppression to actively promoting liberation at all the levels described above. Again, as noted earlier, psychology has a tendency to focus on the individual level in isolation.

article continues after advertisement

Key for Prilleltensky, is increasing and integrating political awareness—educating communities, fostering their psychopolitical literacy so individuals and groups are better able to critically understand and challenge the systems that sustain inequality and inequity. Helping people understand how individual difficulties are connected to broader social and political structures. Equipping people and communities with the tools to resist and reshape the conditions that harm them.

Special Issue

Five years after the 2003 article, a special issue on PPV was published in the Journal of Community Psychology. Prilleltensky expanded on his original work, as quoted above, to explore not just oppression, but the promotion of wellness and liberation. A number of commentaries were also published.

One of the commentaries was by Dennis Fox, a collaborator with whom Prilleltensky wrote two editions of the textbook: “Critical psychology: An introduction” (1997, 2009). In his commentary, Fox emphasizes the potential importance of prioritizing PPV’s practical value rather than becoming overly preoccupied with its theoretical purity. Attempting to perfectly define PPV might, he notes, distract from its real purpose: supporting meaningful action and social change.

Fox highlights their history, together, of trying to push a more political, power-aware, justice-focused agenda within both community psychology and psychology more generally. Fox also cites the work of others who had tried to do this before them. He notes how all this work had resulted in: “publication in prestigious journals, congratulatory letters, citation by others coming after us, but not much institutional change” (p.233). Also highlighting how: “it’s important to keep in mind that psychology’s vast mainstream still pays little attention to its own radical critics” (p.233).

More provocatively, Fox asks whether institutions, including psychological ones, may themselves be part of the problem? Wondering whether radical change, if it is going to come at all, may need to come from outside of psychology.

At the time of writing, Prilleltensky’s 2008 article has been cited nearly 1,000 times on Google Scholar and the second edition of their Critical Psychology textbook more than 1,300. Yet despite this influence, how many psychologists are familiar with the idea of psychopolitical validity? And how many routinely apply its epistemic and transformative lenses to their work?

article continues after advertisement

Definitions

Finally, the piece above uses certain terms which are worth briefly defining using quotes from the original articles.

Power: “the capacity and opportunity to fulfill or obstruct personal, relational or collective needs” (2008, p.119). Note how, in this definition, power is neutral. It can lead to oppression, but can also promote wellness and liberation.

Oppression: “a state of asymmetric power relations characterized by domination, subordination, and resistance” (2003, p.195).

Liberation: “the process of resisting oppressive forces and striving toward psychological and political well-being” (2003, p.195).

Wellness: “Wellness is achieved by the simultaneous, balanced, and contextually sensitive satisfaction of personal, relational, and collective needs (2008, p.122). Notice that this is not merely individual happiness.

item.title: The 'Moving at the Speed of Trust' Test
item.description:
Leadership

The 'Moving at the Speed of Trust' Test

A common leadership phrase can have different meanings.

Posted July 30, 2026

Key points
  • The phrase "moving at the speed of trust" can carry real meaning.
  • It breaks down into three meanings, and each carries its own implications.
  • Trust can be an accelerant, a risk-dampener, and woven into the work fabric.
  • Alignment around that powerful slogan can turn it into an operating plan.

I have heard truisms about trust over the years. This one, "moving at the speed of trust," I recently (re)heard from two different business leaders, and both times it was offered as though its meaning were self-evident. But as you watch companies try to implement technology, especially healthcare devices, digital tools, and AI, you realize people are using the exact same phrase to justify entirely different behaviors.

Having studied consumer trust for over three decades, I decided to figure out what this phrase might mean for implementation in healthcare. That is the purpose of this short blog.

My summary finding is that the phrase, or mission statement, breaks down into three meanings, and each carries its own implications for how you implement, cash flow requirements and timing, investor communications, and what challenges you should expect. A firm could even be following all three at once. When leadership and implementation teams are not aligned on which meaning is in play, friction is inevitable.

Moving at the speed of trust: A choice
Source: Mary Grace / Unsplash

Meaning 1: Trust as a precondition and an accelerant

Here the firm builds a credibility signature before the work begins, using everything at its disposal: prior experience, the backgrounds and biographies of the founders and leaders, formal credentials, and the robustness of the validation behind the technology itself. The purpose of that signature is to de-risk what follows.

article continues after advertisement

New technology inside an organization often asks a great deal of people, and can even be threatening. It asks them to modify their behavior, it may call for sacrifice or cost cutting, and its promise may be uncertain or only half understood. Initially conveyed trust smooths the pathway into the first discussions, the implementation, and each next step. When trust is high at the front door, decisions happen faster and you avoid endless consensus-building later. A clinician who arrives carrying a respected credential enjoys exactly this kind of trust. So too can a technology implementation team.

Meaning 2: Go slow first to go fast later

In this case, the firm treats the initial phase of an engagement as the trust-building phase. You lean toward safety, make the careful call rather than the quick one, and accept the cost of a slower early process even when opportunity is knocking. You may also absorb the cost of early failures rather than passing them along, or invest the opening period in validation work, safety studies, and evidence that precedes any commercial push.

What you are communicating in this period is your posture: that you are benevolent, that you are reliable, that you are the kind of partner who takes on risk rather than transferring it. Once that early work has dampened the risk, both sides can speed up together, and the speed that follows rests on a foundation of confidence.

Meaning 3: Build trust as you build the solution

Under this approach, implementation never runs ahead of the confidence that has been earned. You go no faster than your relationships can sustain, and you do not outrun the consent of the people you are building with, even if your technology roadmap technically could. It is neither as fast as the first path nor as slow as the second, and it requires careful, continuous tending. The trust it produces is durable, because it is earned inside the customer’s own operational experience rather than in your marketing.

This is the classic way any relationship forms: the clinician who earns trust during and through the visits themselves, one encounter at a time, rather than through anything brought to the first appointment. I suspect this third meaning continues regardless of which of the other two you adopt, because trust does not arrive in a punctuated phase with a dead end. You do not communicate trust at the outset and then race ahead unchecked, and you do not go slow for a season and then race ahead unchecked.

article continues after advertisement

Why does it matter to sort this out? Nailing down your exact approach matters for four key reasons:

  • Naming your path provides operational logic. Putting some teeth under the statement, with examples of how your particular firm does it, ironically builds trust in your actual strategy.
  • The three paths run on different timelines. The signals you should read, and the specific KPIs that tell you whether the approach is working, differ across them.
  • The cash flows differ in magnitude and timing. Each path asks investors for a different kind of patience, and that request should be made knowingly.
  • Strategy works better named than implied. Understanding the trade-offs you are taking on, and aligning the entire organization around a shared reality, always beats an empowering mission with no operational logic underneath it.

So when the phrase next comes up in a meeting, ask which of the three meanings is actually on the table, and whether everyone present would give the same answer. Alignment around that powerful slogan can turn it into an operating plan, and ensure the leaders are using the same meaning as the teams.

item.title: Get What’s on the Inside Out
item.description:
Creativity

Get What’s on the Inside Out

Vitality requires self-expression—of your voice, values, passions, and creativity.

Posted July 30, 2026

Key points
  • The drive for self-expression is an ancient and innate hunger, and the health of mind and body depend on it.
  • Passions unlived, creative urges stifled, and truths unspoken are self-expressions that are being suppressed.
  • Start with the subtlest impulses to express yourself, and build from there.
Source: Kei_Therapeutic_Art/Pixabay

“If you ask me what I came into this world to do, I will tell you. I came to live out loud.” —Emile Zola

I met a young man some years ago who told me that he’d always wanted to be a teacher and speaker, but spent so many years “biting my tongue” that he literally had a pronounced scar on the tip of his tongue, like a big callous, from where he’d bitten it repeatedly.

Whether your own yearning for self-expression involves teaching, dancing, leadership, community-building, or running a restaurant, the hunger is the same: to get what’s on the inside out. To make the invisible visible, to speak your mind, to let your cats out of the bag. And you’re driven to sate this innate hunger to be true to yourself as the most naturally expressive of creatures, for the sheer pleasure and self-satisfaction of it, and to make contact with the larger hive—to be heard, seen, witnessed.

In a sense, everything you do is an expression of who you are, from the shoes you wear to the way you raise your children, spend your time, solve your problems, react to suffering or joy, and do the work you do. The question is, are these expressions of who you really are, which is a centrifugal force pushing out from within, a bird flapping against its cage?

When performance artist Nina Wise asks students what brings them to her improv classes, they talk of something missing in their lives, a longing to rekindle self-expression, spontaneity, and play—the turbines of creativity. They want to lift the lids they’ve clamped over their lives, beneath which are great balls of fire—energy, emotions, expressiveness, passion, contribution.

What they’re ultimately after, she says, is “delivering the truth.” And whether you deliver it through words, images, or sounds, through art, innovation, or improvisation, you release the heat of the spirit and say yes to what wants to emerge in your life.

To express means to push outward, to press into being: not just to transmit but to reveal, the way tears reveal grief and dreams reveal desires. Expression is e-motion. It’s pro-creation. It’s giving birth not only to your passions, visions, and talents, but to yourself, unearthing and sharing your deepest authenticity, if not the deeper voices that want to speak through you, which are also trying to push their way into the world—your Buddha nature, your Christ consciousness, your True Self.

And if your true self isn’t being expressed, it’s likely being suppressed or repressed or depressed, which all mean the same thing—pushed down. And what’s pushed down doesn’t tend to obediently stay down. It tends to come up somewhere else in your life, urgent and rebellious.

If delivering the truth has its risks, so does not delivering it. Passions unlived, gifts ungiven, creative urges chloroformed, even secrets unspoken, are things you’re withholding or restraining, and they tend to build up a charge that needs discharging.

article continues after advertisement

And discharging it can be flat-out healing. Social psychologist James Pennebaker, a pioneer of writing therapy, found that expressing your thoughts and feelings about an event (or even trauma) brings on healing, from a drop in blood pressure and heart rate to a boost in immune function and general outlook.

The world, however, and your own psyche, aren’t always so friendly to “delivering the truth,” and frankly, life can be so full of deterrents to self-expression and authenticity that what we casually refer to as “normal” behavior could really be seen as a state of arrested development. To be sure, self-expression doesn’t happen without continual negotiation between bridle and spur, inhibition and exhibition.

I run into this regularly in my freewriting practice, which I do to keep the creative machinery oiled and generate material. What I’m attempting to do is stream-of-consciousness writing, taking as my mottos “garbage is good” and “quantity leads to quality.” But I’m seldom able to overcome the bad habit of editing while I write, the critic effectively steaming up the creator’s glasses during the act of creation.

Sometimes I come around. I turn to the critic and say: “You. Out. When the creator is finished, then you can come in and do your thing, but not until then. Otherwise, I’m driving with one foot on the gas and the other on the brake, and it’s having a constipating effect on my work. It’s the opposite of free-writing.”

If you're not used to expressing yourself, though (creatively or emotionally), then you're probably going to have to start by forcing yourself. To get up from the couch, put on some music, and dance. To write poetry on restaurant napkins and sing in the shower. To take your poems and jokes out to open-mic night. To try telling a loved one what's really on your mind. That is, start with the subtlest impulses to express yourself, and build from there.

article continues after advertisement

And if you want a visual aid to understand how bridle and spur, brake and accelerator, operate in your life, consider this exercise: Have a friend interview you on camera about the level of self-expression in various arenas of your life—creative, vocational, social, and romantic. Touch on the dreams or disappointments you have around them, what you’re doing versus what you’d like to be doing, the pros and cons of your various choices, and even what advice you receive from your body, mind, and spirit.

The point is to get you talking freely for at least half an hour.

Then get a group of friends together on a Friday night, make popcorn, watch the video together, and let them give you feedback on what they see. Because what you’ll see will be an outpouring of raw data about how you truly feel about your involvements and creativities, or lack thereof, and your level of authenticity and self-expression. You’ll see changes of posture, gesture, energy, and expression. You’ll see the lights come on in your eyes when you’re impassioned, and go out when you’re not. And you’ll see what’s on the inside that wants out.

item.title: Unpacking the Invisible Moving Boxes
item.description:
Emotional Labor

Unpacking the Invisible Moving Boxes

The emotional and administrative weight of changing addresses.

Posted July 30, 2026

Key points
  • The unseen burdens of moving include emotional and administrative work.
  • Parents become shock absorbers and teachers as they find themselves explaining the moving process.
  • Structure, shared tasks, and predictable routines help tame the overwhelming chaos of a move.

Summer is the main season for moving. Boxes have been bought, taped, and loaded, and the physical reality of moving is all bubble-wrapped and tightly stuffed. Some people ask friends to help carry couches in exchange for pizza, while others gasped at the price and then paid the movers for full service. Even though everyone has estimated time and measured doorways, somehow miscalculations occur.

Long before the first roll of tape is unraveled and long after the last box is unpacked, there is an entire layer of unnoticed labor involved: the invisible work of moving. And until you are in the thick of it, you have no idea, or have forgotten, how heavy the workload is. From the endless administrative paperwork to the waves of emotions, the work compounds.

The Labyrinth of Moving Paperwork

Moving becomes a full-time administrative position, just with higher stakes. More than just signatures, the paperwork demands your timeliness and hypervigilance. You are a forensic accountant digging up bank statements or tax returns, proving where a gift transfer came from, and deciphering the foreign language of insurance. You may find yourself signing disclosures for a water line you’ve never even seen, reviewing Docusigns at midnight, or learning how to do a wire transfer for the first time.

When you are moving with children, this administrative footprint quadruples. You aren’t just transferring a life; you are transferring an ecosystem—requesting official school records, booking pediatrician appointments, filling out dozens of emergency contact forms, researching who accepts your updated insurance plan, and finding out if they are accepting new patients.

Separately, each form, whether for you or your family, is a small, mundane task, but stacked together, they form a mountain of cognitive overload. Every pending email or unsent record can become a micro-stressor quietly humming in the background of your mind while you try to remember your next task or where you packed the coffee maker.

Fresh Starts Still May Have Grieving Hearts

The true unseen burden of moving is not the physical effort of lifting boxes or the mental load of administrative paperwork; it is the emotional toll required to dismantle one's life and reconstruct another. Typically, moving is surrounded by forward momentum language like “new beginnings” and “exciting chapters,” but what about those visible height marks on the pantry door or that familiar squeak on the third step of your stairwell? It is the grief of saying goodbye to the places and people that shaped you, buried beneath the urgency of closing dates and utility setups. It is the mental load of keeping track of a hundred moving parts while maintaining a calm exterior for you, your coworkers, and/or your children. It is the silent work of making a strange new space feel like home, one small, intentional step at a time.

article continues after advertisement

Those with dependents, particularly parents, become a shock absorber. You also become a full-time teacher of transition as you find yourself explaining abstract concepts like “keeping in touch” and “long distance.” Research published in the Journal of Sociology & Social Welfare and the Journal of Happiness Studies notes that moving creates acute stress for developing minds as children process transitions through a lens of powerlessness. Overnight, their environment, their routine, and their social circles may change. When a child throws a tantrum over a mislaid toy during the move, you know it isn’t about the toy. It is about the loss of control. So, you absorb the outburst, set aside your own exhaustion, and hold space for their anxiousness or anger. This emotional labor has no paper trail, yet it demands more energy than packing or unpacking an entire kitchen.

How to Tame the Invisible Load of Moving

While the administrative and emotional weight of relocating cannot be eliminated, structure can help turn overwhelming chaos into manageable steps:

  1. Share the Cognitive Load
    1. Create a “control center” document to track deadlines and account information. Note all the tasks and divide and delegate accordingly.
  2. Lean on Your Routine and Relationships
    1. Protect care routines. Maintain consistent mealtimes, bedtime rituals, workouts, or morning habits throughout the transition. Predictability in schedules balances the external unpredictability of moving and new surroundings.
    2. Create opportunities for closure and acknowledge that the end of a chapter makes space for the next. Have that goodbye social. Take photos of your favorite spots. Keep a memory stone. Make notes in your journal.
  3. Restore Agency in Dependents
    1. Invite them to contribute. Allow them to make micro-decisions to increase their autonomy. Restoring control minimizes relocation anxiety, so let them choose a wall color or select a new theme for their bedroom.
    2. Prioritize their space. Establishing a recognizable safe haven helps ground them in the new space.
article continues after advertisement

So, this summer, whether you, a neighbor, or a coworker is moving, consider honoring yourself by taking your regularly scheduled yoga class in the midst of the move, bringing your new neighbor a meal, or making your departing friend a care package for their ride. Because in the end, when the last box is unpacked and the pictures are finally hung on the wall, no one gives out awards for the administrative hours logged, the emotional meltdowns navigated, or the quiet tears shed during a move. It is invisible, heavy, and exhausting; however, it is also the truest measure of the care we put into building a life.
